title: Are You Maxxing Your Curiosity?
author: Marc Smith
summary: Marc Smith notices that his social media feed now includes university students sharing learning advice under the banner of curiositymaxxing, a counterpoint to talk of falling IQs and brain rot. Although he dislikes internet buzzwords, he argues the label points to something real: epistemic curiosity, the intrinsic drive to fill gaps in knowledge and reduce uncertainty. He offers a working definition of curiositymaxxing as the deliberate and sustained pursuit of knowledge in response to things we want to know but do not yet understand. He distinguishes trait curiosity from state curiosity and links the former to Need for Cognition, noting that curiosity peaks in childhood, dips in adulthood, and resurges later. He asks whether the trend simply promotes knowledge without understanding, but finds that much of the advice, such as returning to material over the following week, rests on sound learning science about retrieval and effort. His conclusion is that short videos are only curiosity triggers, and the real curiositymaxxers are those who follow up by reading, studying, and working through material.
points: Curiositymaxxing can be defined as the deliberate and sustained pursuit of knowledge in response to things we want to know but do not yet understand, which makes it more than accumulating facts.
Epistemic curiosity is the drive to fill a gap in understanding, and it varies across the lifespan and between people as both a trait and a fleeting state.
Some of the student advice online is grounded in learning science, for example the insistence on returning to content over the following week to harness retrieval and mental effort.
Learning a subject in a day is unrealistic because the learning brain prefers snacking to gorging.
Short social media posts are curiosity triggers only; the benefit comes from following up with books and courses, which separates true curiositymaxxers from passive scrollers.
quotes: Curiositymaxxing is certainly about knowledge accumulation, but that downplays the nature of both knowledge creation and epistemic curiosity (the intrinsic desire to acquire new information and to reduce uncertainty).
Curiosity attempts to fill a gap in our knowledge and understanding, so it’s more than simply the desire to know things. It also changes across the lifespan.
the deliberate and sustained pursuit of knowledge in response to the things we want to know but do not yet understand.
Trait curiosity correlates with another trait known as Need for Cognition; the desire to engage in and enjoyment of tasks that involve high mental effort.
And does curiositymaxxing simply advocate an increase in knowledge in the absence of understanding, resulting in shallow learning and poorly developed knowledge networks?

There was also a huge caveat: Erin insists you need to return to the content over the following week, invoking the long-standing research on memory, learning, and the power of retrieval and mental effort.

Social media posts are short, so they need to be viewed as a curiosity trigger rather than a means to increase knowledge. You still have to follow the advice, read the book, or work through the online course to reap the benefits.
